newsitem.title: FRANCE: French far-rightist Le Pen claims growing strength.
newsitem.headline: French far-rightist Le Pen claims growing strength.

text.p: French far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen boasted on Monday that his espousal of racial inequality had boosted his National Front, and accused mainstream parties of plotting to drive him from politics.

"What are they going to do to me? Gas me? Assassinate me? Machine-gun me? What can they do to force people to vote for the 'Gang of Four'?" he asked in a television interview, referring to the four mainstream parties.

In local by-election run-offs on Sunday, candidates from the governing centre-right edged out the Front with support from the Left in the southern city of Toulon and in Chaville in suburban Paris after the Front candidate led in first-round voting.
Mainstream politicians hailed the Left's decision to support rightist candidates via a so-called "Republican Front" intended to keep Le Pen's backers out of office.
But they also acknowledged that the Front's scores were higher than in previous elections in those districts.
In addition, in the Riviera capital Nice, the Front candidate led the field after an initial round of voting on Sunday for a departmental council post.
"This is a major victory," Le Pen, who scored 15 percent in last year's presidential elections, told France 2 television.
In Chaville, the government-backed candidate "was saved only by Socialist and Communist votes," defeated National Front contender Sophie Brissaud said in a statement thanking backers.
"Every day more French pople are giving their support to the National Front," she said. "Our growing strength is inevitable."
Le Pen accused the government of trying to cripple him with a plan to strengthen French laws against inciting racial hatred.

Justice Minister Jacques Toubon prepared draft legislation for parliament after concluding that existing laws were too weak to prosecute Le Pen for stating this month that racial inequality was "obvious" and "a fact".
Le Pen called the draft a "totalitarian law...that obviously targets the National Front".
But he was not alone in his criticisms of the plan.

Senator and ex-interior minister Charles Pasqua said attacking Le Pen in the courts would only send the Front leader higher in the opinion polls. "We are playing into Le Pen's hands," he told TF1 television on Sunday.

"In a democratic society, what can be condemned on moral grounds does not always meet up exactly with what can be condemned on legal grounds," the international press watchdog group Reporters sans Frontieres (Reporters without Borders) said.
The group warned that the bill's broad language could dismantle existing protections on freedom of speech and urged Toubon to withdraw it.
Le Pen, who last week had urged Prime Minister Alain Juppe to resign, also cranked up his rhetoric against Juppe, calling him "a huckster, anti-national and a criminal against humanity".
Le Pen had last week urged Juppe to resign after the prime minister called Le Pen "deeply, almost viscerally racist, antisemitic and xenophobic".

Le Pen said the government's tactics showed its "formidable weakness" due to its inability to solve the problems considered most important by the French people, which he identified as unemployment, immigration and insecurity.
"I intend in the days ahead to fight back, and to press the National Front's advantage," he said.
